Appendix B

  • Bond1 network configuration


    The following YAML file is a Bond1 network configuration YAML file. Use this file to create and apply the configuration on the OpenShift cluster.

    $ vi bond1-config.yaml
apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1
kind: NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy
metadata:
  name: bond1-configurations-on-all-nodes
spec:
  desiredState:
    interfaces:
    - name: bond1
       description: Bond with ports ens3f0np0 and ens3f1np1
      type: bond
      state: up
      ipv4:
        dhcp: false
        enabled: false
       link-aggregation:
        mode: 802.3ad
        options:
          miimon: '100'
        port:
        - ens3f0np0
        - ens3f1np1
      mtu: 9000
$ oc apply -f bond1-config.yaml

Appendix B

  • VLAN tagging on the bond interface


    The following sample YAML file is a VLAN tagging network configuration file. Use this file to create and apply the configuration on the OpenShift cluster

    $ vi vlan_tagging_bond1.yaml
apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1
kind: NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy
metadata:
  name: ocpnode1-bond1-vlans
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: "node3.ocp18.bdcrack13.local"
  desiredState:
    interfaces:
      - name: bond1.151
        description: PowerFlex Data 1 VLAN151 
        type: vlan
        state: up
        ipv4:
          address:
            - ip: 192.168.151.223
              prefix-length: 24
          enabled: true
        vlan:
          base-iface: bond1
          id: 151
        mtu: 9000
      - name: bond1.152
        description: PowerFlex Data 2 VLAN152
        type: vlan
        state: up
        ipv4:
          address:
            - ip: 192.168.152.223
              prefix-length: 24
          enabled: true
        vlan:
          base-iface: bond1
          id: 152
        mtu: 9000 
      - name: bond1.154
        description: VM live migration on VLAN154 
        type: vlan
        state: up
        ipv4:
          address:
            - ip: 192.168.154.223
              prefix-length: 24
          enabled: true
        vlan:
          base-iface: bond1
          id: 154
        mtu: 9000

$ oc apply -f vlan_tagging_bond1.yaml

Appendix B

  • Bridge interface on the VLAN interface


    The following sample YAML file is a bridge interface network configuration on the VLAN interface on one of the nodes. Create and apply a similar configuration to all the nodes by changing the hostname in the kubernetes.io/hostname" parameter.

    $ cat bridge_node1_config.yaml
apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1
kind: NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy
metadata:
  name: node1-br1-eth1-policy
spec:
  nodeSelector:
     kubernetes.io/hostname: "node3.ocp18.bdcrack13.local"
  desiredState:
    interfaces:
      - name: node1.br154
         description: Linux bridge with bond1.154 as a port for VM live migration
        type: linux-bridge
        state: up
        ipv4:
        - ip: 192.168.154.244
           prefix-length: 24
           enabled: true
        bridge:
           options:
            stp:
               enabled: false
          port:
            - name: bond1.154
$ oc apply -f bridge_node1_config.yaml

Appendix B

  • NAD configuration

    The following sample YAML file is a Network Attachment Definition (NAD) file on one of the bridge interfaces. This file will be used to configure the network on VMs. Create a similar configuration for each of the bridge interfaces and apply it to the cluster.

    $ vi nad-config-154.yaml
apiVersion: "k8s.cni.cncf.io/v1"
kind: NetworkAttachmentDefinition
metadata:
  name: nad-154
  annotations:
     k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/resourceName: bridge.network.kubevirt.io/br1
spec:
  config: |
    {
       "cniVersion": "0.3.1",
       "name": "bridge-network",
       "type": "bridge",
       "bridge": "node1.br154",
       "macspoofchk": false,
       "vlan": 154,
       "disableContainerInterface": true,
       "preserveDefaultVlan": false
    }
 
$ oc apply -f nad-config-154.yaml

Best practices

  • PowerFlex cluster

    For the PowerFlex cluster:

    • Verify that SDS threads is set to twelve. To check this value using PowerFlex CLI, run the following command on the primary MDM node: scli --set_performance_parameters --all_sds --tech --sds_number_os_threads 12
    • Separate the management and data traffic from production application traffic. This separation can be done using VLANs. For more information, see the following documentation:
      • Post-installation activities
      • Dell EMC PowerFlex: Networking Best Practices and Design Considerations.

Best practices

  • OpenShift Virtualization


    For OpenShift Virtualization:

    • If possible, use the golden images provided by Red Hat when creating VMs. These images are secure images that make the VM configuration process faster and more efficient. See Creating a VM using golden images.
    • Monitor VM CPU, memory, and storage consumption in the performance dashboard page to identify potential bottlenecks and optimize resource allocation if necessary.
    • Implement a backup and restore strategy for your provisioned VMs to ensure data protection.
    • Use the XFS file system for workloads if you want to run databases on OpenShift VMs. Set the default file system as XFS in the CSI values.yaml file and set the default CSI storage class as vxflexos-xfs.
    • If possible, configure VM live migration on a separate physical NIC.

Configure the networks on the compute nodes

Dell.com Contact Us
Share
United States/English

Home > Storage > PowerFlex > White Papers > Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization with Dell PowerFlex > Configure the networks on the compute nodes

Configure the networks on the compute nodes

  • To configure the preceding networks on the compute nodes, perform the following steps. After every step, verify that the configuration is applied successfully and is in the available state by running the oc get nncp command.

    1. Create a second bond interface (bond1) using one port from each of the network cards. 
      The bond0 interface that you created during the cluster installation handles the OpenShift Ingress/API traffic, while the bond1 interface handles all the remaining traffic, including PowerFlex management and data traffic. The sample YAML file in Bond1 network configuration in Appendix B shows the configuration of bond1 on the nodes.
    2. Create a VLAN interface for each of the required networks on the configured bond interfaces. 
      See the sample YAML file in VLAN tagging on the bond interface in Appendix B, which shows the configuration of the VLAN interface on bond1 for guidance. A VLAN interface must be defined for every node.

    For more information, see the following documentation:

    • Configuring networks using NNCP: Updating node network configuration
    • OpenShift networking: Configuring and managing cluster networking

    Note: Optionally consider placing a VM Migration VLAN on a separate NIC.

Executive summary


  • Application platforms that combine support for both traditional virtual machines (VMs) and lightweight technologies such as containers are of particular interest for organizations that want to get ahead. The transition to containerized network functions is an ongoing process. In the short term, deployment and management of workloads running on VMs is required. Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization unifies the operations and management of VMs and containers on the same platform, helping organizations to benefit from their existing investments in virtualization.

    Dell PowerFlex is a software-defined infrastructure that is designed to reduce operational and infrastructure complexity, empowering organizations to move faster by delivering flexibility, elasticity, and simplicity with predictable performance and resiliency at scale. The PowerFlex family provides a foundation that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed, unified fabric. PowerFlex also provides stable and predictable performance for all workloads, including high-performance databases.

    This paper provides guidance for the deployment and configuration of a Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization solution using PowerFlex as the underlying software-defined infrastructure. The paper also describes cases such as cloning, live migration, and snapshots of VMs on OpenShift Virtualization along with Dell Container Storage Interface (CSI) for streamlined operations.

Home > Storage > PowerFlex > White Papers > Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization with Dell PowerFlex > Installing OpenShift Virtualization using the web console

Installing OpenShift Virtualization using the web console

  • To install OpenShift virtualization using the web console:

    1. From the Administrator perspective, click Operators > OperatorHub.
    2. In the Filter by keyword field, enter OpenShift Virtualization.
    3. Select the OpenShift Virtualization tile.
    4. Read the information about the Operator and click Install.
    5. On the Install Operator page:
      1. Select stable from the list of available Update Channel options. This ensures that you install the version of OpenShift Virtualization that is compatible with your OpenShift Container Platform version.
      2. For Installed Namespace, ensure that the Operator recommended namespace option is selected. This installs the Operator in the mandatory openshift-cnv namespace, which is automatically created if it does not exist.
      3. For Approval Strategy, it is highly recommended that you select the default value of Automatic so that OpenShift Virtualization automatically updates when a new version is available in the stable update channel.
      4. Click Install to make the Operator available to the openshift-cnv namespace.
      5. When the Operator installs successfully, click Create HyperConverged.
      6. Click Create to launch OpenShift Virtualization.

Logical architecture

  • The following diagram shows the logical architecture of this solution:

    Table 4. Logical design of OpenShift virtualization on Dell PowerFlex

     

    PowerFlex Manager is used to deploy a PowerFlex storage-only (SO) cluster on four bare metal servers.

    A single PowerFlex protection domain and a single storage pool are configured on PowerFlex. The PowerFlex storage pool topology consists of four SDSs with 10 SSD disks in each of the four SDS nodes.

    An OpenShift cluster with three control nodes and three worker nodes is deployed using OpenShift Assisted Installer. After the cluster deployment, the required PowerFlex networks are configured on these OpenShift nodes.

    Next, the PowerFlex CSI driver is installed. The PowerFlex Storage Data Client (SDC) is automatically installed by the CSI driver installation on the OpenShift worker nodes. The CSI driver for PowerFlex provides support for provisioning persistent storage using the PowerFlex storage cluster. For more information, see Installing the CSI Driver for PowerFlex.

Network architecture

  • Additional network configuration is required on the OpenShift nodes to enable the nodes to connect to the PowerFlex cluster. For example, you can add or remove network interfaces by applying a NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy  (NNCP) manifest to the cluster.

    Note: The Kubernetes NMState Operator must be installed in the OpenShift cluster to enable use of the NNCP manifest. For more information, see Kubernetes NMState.

    The following diagram shows the network architecture of this solution:

    Figure 5. Network architecture

     

    Each PowerFlex SO node is connected to the TOR switches. All nodes are equipped with dual-port NICs, and these network ports are trunked with the TOR switches. The NICs handle management, data1, data2, data3, and data4 network traffic for PowerFlex. The management network operates in active-backup (mode1) bonding with the data1 and data2 networks, while the data3 and data4 networks are dedicated SDS networks and are not bonded. This network configuration provides redundancy and fault tolerance, with two dedicated networks for PowerFlex data transfer. 

    Dedicated VLANs are used to separate management and data network traffic. The following table shows the different VLANs that are used for PowerFlex SO nodes along with their respective purposes:

OpenShift deployment prerequisites

  • A healthy OpenShift cluster must be up and running before you install OpenShift Virtualization.

    Ensure that the following requirements are met before deploying an OpenShift cluster:

    • DNS: Records for ingress and API Virtual IP addresses are required for accessing the cluster. However, because such Virtual IP addresses are managed by the cluster itself, no external load balancer is required.
    • SSH public key: Generate this key on the workstation from where the nodes will be accessed. This key will be used to authenticate SSH access to the nodes: for example, for troubleshooting during deployment or for longer-term maintenance post-deployment. For more information, see Generating a key pair for cluster node SSH access.
    • NTP server: This server is required for time synchronization among hosts.
    • For this architecture, as part of the network requirements and because this deployment is the “connected” type, all the OpenShift cluster nodes must have connectivity to the Internet.

    Note: To install OpenShift in a disconnected environment, follow the instructions in Installing a cluster in a disconnected environment.

    For more information, see OpenShift assisted Installer prerequisites.

OpenShift Virtualization

  • OpenShift Virtualization, an included feature of Red Hat OpenShift, provides a modern platform for organizations to run and deploy their new and existing VM workloads. The solution allows for easy migration and management of traditional VMs onto a trusted, consistent, and comprehensive hybrid cloud application platform.

    OpenShift Virtualization enables the following virtualization tasks: 

    • Creating and managing Linux and Windows VMs
    • Connecting to VMs through a variety of consoles and CLI tools
    • Importing and cloning existing VMs
    • Managing network interface controllers and storage disks attached to VMs
    • Live migrating VMs between nodes

    OpenShift Virtualization simplifies the migration of your VMs while offering a path for infrastructure modernization, taking advantage of the simplicity and speed of a cloud-native application platform. It aims to preserve existing virtualization investments while embracing modern management principles, and it is the foundation for Red Hat’s comprehensive virtualization solution.

    For more information, see OpenShift Virtualization.

OpenShift Virtualization architecture

  • OpenShift Virtualization is an add-on to OpenShift Container Platform that allows you to run and manage VM workloads alongside container workloads. OpenShift Virtualization is based on upstream KubeVirt , which implements the deployment and management of VMs using Kubernetes constructs such as PVCs and pods. The following figure shows the KubeVirt components that are implemented in OpenShift Virtualization:

    Figure 3. OpenShift Virtualization architecture

     

     The KubeVirt components of OpenShift Virtualization are:

    • virt-controller: An operator that detects when new VM resources are created and creates the corresponding pod in which the VM will run. After the pod is scheduled to a node, virt-controller provides the VM object with the node name and hands off to the virt-handler.
    • virt-handler: A daemon set running on every compute node, which performs all the steps that are required to move a VM object to the p state. This task is performed by referencing the VM specification and then creating a libvirtd domain on the VM pod. In the context of VMs, "p-state" refers to a processor's performance state, which dictates its operating frequency and voltage, allowing for dynamic adjustments to power consumption and performance based on workload demands. Virt-handler turns off the corresponding domain after the VM object is deleted.
    • virt-launcher: As the primary container running on every VM pod, this component creates the necessary cgroups and namespaces to host a VM after it is provided with a VM object to deploy from virt-handler. An instance of libvirtd hosted within virt-launcher is used to create the VM. After the VM is created, virt-launcher waits until the VM process is completed and then terminates itself. Virt-launcher also attempts to prevent preemptive shutdowns from Kubernetes to ensure that the VM has exited before virt-launcher terminates.
    • libvirtd: An instance of libvirtd exists in every VM pod and is used by virt-launcher to manage the life cycle of the VM object.

    For more information, see OpenShift virtualization architecture.

Postinstallation configuration

  • Node placement

    It is recommended that you keep the default scheduling of VMs on the worker node. You can specify the nodes to which you want the workloads, operators, and controllers deployed by configuring node placement rules for the following tasks:

    • Deploy VMs only on nodes intended for virtualization workloads.
    • Deploy Operators only on infrastructure nodes.
    • Maintain separation between workloads.

    This solution assumes use of the default scheduling of workloads and does not apply any changes to node placement configuration. If you want to perform node placement, ensure that you adhere to the node placement rules.

Postinstallation configuration

  • Network configuration

    By default, OpenShift Virtualization is installed with a single internal pod network. For additional network configuration, the following operators are required:

    • Kubernetes NMState Operator: This operator is used to configure the Linux bridge network that can be used for live migration or for providing external access to VMs. Follow the steps in Installing the Kubernetes NMState Operator.
    • The SR-IOV Operator: This operator manages the SR-IOV network devices. To install the SR-IOV network operator, follow Installing the SR-IOV Network Operator.
    • The MetalLB Operator: This operator enables the creation of load balancing services by using the OpenShift Container Platform web console. To install the MetalLB operator, follow the steps in Installing the MetalLB Operator.
    • The bond1.154 interface: As described in Network configuration, the bond1.154interface is useful in VM live migration. To add this network for live migration to the VMs, perform the following steps:
    1. Configure a bridge interface on the VLAN interfaces. See the sample YAML file showing the configuration of bridge interface on the VLAN interface.
    2. Configure the Network Attachment Definition (NAD) file for each of the VLAN interfaces which will be used to configure the network on the VMs. See the sample YAML file showing the configuration of a NAD file using the bridge interface that you configured in the preceding step.

PowerFlex consumption options

  • PowerFlex rack

    PowerFlex rack is a software-defined infrastructure platform that combines compute as well as high-performance storage resources in a managed unified network. This rack-based engineered system, with integrated networking, enables customers to achieve the scalability and management requirements of a modern data center.

    PowerFlex appliance

    PowerFlex appliance is a PowerEdge-based server which has been configured to be a node in a software-defined storage deployment that runs PowerFlex software components. This offering allows customers the flexibility and savings to bring their own compatible networking or make use of full network automation using a supported set of Dell or Cisco switches.

    PowerFlex custom nodes

    PowerFlex Custom Nodes are validated server building-blocks configured for use with PowerFlex. They are available with thousands of configuration options and are available for customers who prefer to build their own environments.

    PowerFlex in the public cloud

    PowerFlex software storage services can be deployed on recommended instances (with attached storage) in Amazon Web Services or Microsoft Azure. Only the MG data layout and Independent (disaggregated) architecture is supported. Fault Sets may be used to distribute the cluster across multiple Availability Zones (AZ), improving resiliency even during AZ disruptions. Native asynchronous replication may be used to migrate data between cloud and on-premises PowerFlex systems, or to establish cloud-based BC/DR data protection schemes.

PowerFlex CSI/CSM


  • An important component outside of PowerFlex that enables a flexible consumption model for Kubernetes is the PowerFlex CSI driver, developed as a part of the Dell Kubernetes strategy. After loading the CSI driver for PowerFlex into Kubernetes, it can be used to provision persistent volumes from the underlying PowerFlex storage resource. If the Kubernetes deployment is running low on PowerFlex storage resources, you can add PowerFlex storage nodes to increase the system capacity and performance.

    The CSI driver connects the PowerFlex system and Kubernetes deployments. It is a storage broker which dynamically provisions volumes from PowerFlex through the PowerFlex API gateway to the Kubernetes cluster. Once the volume is available on PowerFlex, it is immediately mapped to the requesting pod. If a pod is destroyed or rescheduled, the CSI plug-in ensures that the volumes are remapped upon rescheduling of that pod. 

    Customers running Kubernetes clusters on PowerFlex use the Dell Container Storage Modules (CSM), which extend the CSI driver capabilities. These modules:

    • Provide enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes for cloud-native stateful applications.
    • Reduce management complexity, so that developers can independently use enterprise storage with ease and automate daily operations.
    • Extends storage functionality and capabilities beyond using the CSI driver alone.

    These modules include replication, observability, authorization, application mobility, and resiliency.

    PowerFlex supports multiple operating systems. PowerFlex is validated with the leading Kubernetes distributions as shown in the following figure:

PowerFlex deployment architectures

  • PowerFlex software-defined storage can be deployed in disaggregated (independent compute and storage layers) architectures.

    Independent architecture

    In an independent architecture, or disaggregated architecture, some nodes provide storage capacity for data in applications, while other separate and independent nodes provide compute resources for applications and workloads. Compute and storage resources can be scaled independently by adding nodes to the cluster while it remains active. This separation of compute and storage resources helps to minimize software licensing costs in certain situations. This architecture can be ideal for high-performance databases and application workloads.

    Disaggregation gives organizations the freedom to choose different LCM options that best align with their operational models. Not only can PowerFlex Manager manage the LCM of the PowerFlex storage infrastructure, it can also manage LCM of PowerFlex compute nodes. With this freedom there is also the choice to manage compute estates that connect to PowerFlex with other tooling; for example, VxRail Dynamic Nodes connected to PowerFlex using VxRail Manager automation.

Virtual machines

  • Configuring storage profiles

    A storage profile is allocated for each storage class. The storage profile provides recommended storage settings for the associated storage class. 

    The default StorageClass assigned to this solution is vxflexos, which is used for .OpenShift virtualization disk creation. To assign vxflexos as the default storage class, follow the instructions provided in create storage class. Verify that the default storage class is set to vxflexos, as shown in the following figure:
    Figure 7. Storage class

    To support VM snapshots, ensure that the Volume Snapshot Class is created. Follow the instructions provided in create snapshot class. 

    [root@ocp-admin volumesnapshotclass]# oc create -f snapclass-v1.yaml

    Figure 8. Volume snapshot class

    To specify default parameters, edit the StorageProfile object for the provisioner’s storage class. These default parameters only apply to the persistent volume claim (PVC) only if they are not configured in the DataVolume object.

    $ oc edit storageprofile vxflexos
 
apiVersion: cdi.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: StorageProfile
metadata:
  name: vxflexos
# ...
status:
  claimPropertySets:
  - accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
    volumeMode: Block
  - accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    volumeMode: Block
  - accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    volumeMode: Filesystem
  - accessModes:
    - ReadOnlyMany
    volumeMode: Block
  - accessModes:
    - ReadOnlyMany
    volumeMode: Filesystem
  cloneStrategy: csi-clone
  dataImportCronSourceFormat: pvc
  provisioner: csi-vxflexos.dellemc.com
  storageClass: vxflexos

     You can use storage profiles to set a default cloning method for a storage class. Alternatively, you can edit the storage profile and setting the following attributes:

    apiVersion: cdi.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: StorageProfile
metadata:
  name: vxflexos
# ...
spec:
  claimPropertySets:
  - accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce 
    volumeMode:
      Filesystem 
  cloneStrategy: csi-clone 
status:
  provisioner: csi-vxflexos.dellemc.com
  storageClass: vxflexos

  • Creating a VM using an instance type


    You can also upload your own custom operating system image and create VMs based on this custom image.

    1. Go to Virtualization > Catalog > Instance Types > Add Volume.
    2. In Add volume, select ‘vxflexos’ as the StorageClass so that the uploaded ISO resides in PowerFlex storage.
      This storage acts like persistent storage to all the uploaded operating system images. Upload the custom operating system image, as shown in the following figure:

      Once the operating system is uploaded into the template gallery, you can create a VM.
    3. Go to Virtualization > VirtualMachines > Create > From Instance Type. 
    4. Select the volume to boot from the volume name you uploaded in the previous step.

    5. Select the VM configuration and then click Create VM. 

    You also can create a VM using a YAML file. See the sample VM creationfile.

  • VM cloning


    To clone an existing VM using the web console:

    1. Go to Virtualization > VirtualMachines and select a VM to open the VirtualMachine details page.
    2. Click Actions and select Clone.
    3. On the Clone VirtualMachine page, enter the name of the new VM.
    4. (Optional) Select the Start cloned VM checkbox to start the cloned VM.
    5. Click Clone.

  • Taking VM snapshots

    To take a snapshot of any existing VM using the web console:

    1. Go to Virtualization > VirtualMachines and select a VM. 

      The VirtualMachine details page opens.

    2. Click Actions and select Take Snapshot. 

      The Clone VirtualMachine page opens.

    3. Enter the name of the new VM and click Save, as shown in the following figure:

    Figure 14. taking VM snapshots

    To create snapshots of a VM in the Running state with the highest integrity, install the QEMU guest agent on the VM. The QEMU guest agent takes a consistent snapshot by attempting to quiesce the VM file system. This task ensures that in-flight I/O is written to the disk before the snapshot is taken. For more information, see installing the QEMU guest agent.

  • VM live migration

    Live migration is the process of moving a running VM to another node in the cluster without interrupting the virtual workload. Live migration enables smooth transitions during cluster upgrades or any time that a node needs to be drained for maintenance or configuration changes.

    For live migration, it is recommended to configure a dedicated multus network. In this white paper, VLAN 154 is configured for live migration.

    To configure live migration limits and timeouts, go to Virtualization Settings > General Settings > Live migration.

    You can perform the same configuration by editing the HyperConverged CR using the following code:

    oc edit hyperconverged kubevirt-hyperconverged -n openshift-cnv
          … 
          liveMigrationConfig:
          allowAutoConverge: false
          allowPostCopy: false
          completionTimeoutPerGiB: 800
          network: nad-154
          parallelMigrationsPerCluster: 5
          parallelOutboundMigrationsPerNode: 2
          progressTimeout: 150
          resourceRequirements:
          vmiCPUAllocationRatio: 10
          uninstallStrategy: BlockUninstallIfWorkloadsExist
          virtualMachineOptions:
          disableFreePageReporting: false
          disableSerialConsoleLog: true
          workloadUpdateStrategy:
          batchEvictionInterval: 1m0s
          batchEvictionSize: 10
          workloadUpdateMethods:
          - LiveMigrate
          workloads: {}
          …

    To configure live migration policies for heavy workloads, , see configuration of live migration.

  • VM performance

    This solution uses the workload simulation tool Flexible I/O (FIO) to conduct performance testing on the VMs. The FIO tool measures and analyses the performance of storage media, such as SSD, HDD, or RAID, as well as software-defined storage, such as PowerFlex, by generating different I/O workloads. For more information, see fio tool.

    Specifically, FIO measures:

    • Throughput
    • Latency
    • IOPS
    • Queue depth
    • Read/write performance

    Based on user-defined settings, FIO can produce different types of I/O workloads, from sequential reads to random writes and a mixture of random reads/writes. 

    For the OpenShift virtualization solution, consider these use cases. 

    Use case 1

    In this use case, the FIO tool is run with an 8 K block size and 100 percent read. This workload is often used as a standard benchmark size for assessing read performance, particularly when data is accessed randomly from a cache or storage device. FIO is run on every VM and these VMs are then linearly scaled across three different OpenShift worker nodes. For each VM, an additional disk of 120 GB is attached by editing VM properties. 

    The following FIO command is run on all the VMs simultaneously: 

    fio --name=RandomReadTest_VM1 --readwrite=randread --rwmixwrite=0 --bs=8k --invalidate=1 --direct=1 --filename=/dev/vdb --size=100g --time_based --runtime=600 --ioengine=libaio --numjobs=8 --iodepth=32 --norandommap --randrepeat=0 --exitall --group_reporting



    The graph shows that over a million IOPS with sub millisecond latency can be achieved on three worker nodes.

    Use case 2 

    An 8K block size with a 70/30 read/write ratio (70 percent read, 30 percent write) is commonly used in Online Transaction Processing (OLTP) workloads and databases. This block size and workload profile are a standard for many OLTP applications, including those using database systems such as Oracle. In this case, FIO is run on one VM across each of the OpenShift worker node. 

    The following FIO command is run on all the VMs simultaneously: 

    fio --name=ReadWriteTest --readwrite=randrw --rwmixwrite=30 --bs=8k --invalidate=1 --direct=1 --filename=/dev/vdb --size=100g --time_based --runtime=600 --ioengine=libaio --numjobs=8 --iodepth=32 --norandommap --randrepeat=0 --exitall --group_reporting

    The following table shows the results of running the FIO tool on OpenShift VMs that have been scaled linearly:

    VMs

    1 x VM

    2 x VMs

    3 x VMs

    Read IOPS

    123,362

    225,456

    319,456

    Write IOPS

    53,456

    93,568

    144,251

    Read Latency (ms)

    0.221

    0.238

    0.526

    Write Latency (ms)

    0.241

    0.277

    0.512

    Read Bandwidth (GB/S)

    0.966

    1.766

    2.52

    Write Bandwidth (GB/S)

    0.414

    0.756

    1.08

    The table shows that over a 460,000 IOPS with sub millisecond latency can be achieved on three different VMs.
